【52】There are two variants of pcSMPTCL: indolent and aggressive 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 7 , 8 \]</u>. The vast majority of cases are indolent with small (less than 3 cm) non–progressing solitary lesions, no systemic spread, and a 5-year survival of 90–100 % 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 2 , 4 \]</u>. However, there are reports of very aggressive cases resulting in systemic spread, central nervous system involvement, and death 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 8 \]</u>. Progressive disease and death have been reported in 14 % and 5 % of cases of pcSMPTCL, respectively 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 7 \]</u>. Given the marked difference in prognosis between the indolent and aggressive variants, it is possible that the aggressive form of pcSMPTCL is actually a separate entity; at this time the WHO/EORTC classification system does not differentiate between them 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 2 \]</u>.

### 14.1.2 Prognosis and Treatment|删除换行|pcSMPTCL generally has an excellent prognosis, particularly in patients with solitary or localized lesions 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 , 3 \]</u>. Five-year survival rates range from 60 to 100 % overall 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 2 , 3 \]</u>, with rates of over 90 % for patients with solitary lesions 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 4 \]</u>. The vast majority of patients experience no spread or dissemination of disease, and excision or radiotherapy is often curative 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 3 , 9 \]</u>. Patients with aggressive disease have a median survival of 23 months (range, 18–36 months) 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 8 \]</u>.

Patients with aggressive disease tend to have larger lesions (>5 cm), rapid growth or evolution, ulceration, a high proliferative index, and few CD8+ T cells 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 8 \]</u>.

【55】Given the generally benign nature of this disease, nonaggressive therapy and regular follow-up are recommended 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 3 \]</u>. Surgical excision or radiotherapy is often curative in patients with solitary or localized lesions 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 2 , 3 \]</u>. 【57】### 14.2.1 Histopathology

【58】Skin biopsy demonstrates a dense, nodular or bandlike infiltrate of small to medium pleomorphic mononuclear cells in the dermis and superficial subcutaneous tissue  通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 2 – 4 , 8 \]</u>. Focal epidermotropism is occasionally present 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 6 \]</u>. Many cases show invasion and destruction of pilosebaceous units 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 2 \]</u>.

【49】Chapter 2Dystonia

【50】AbstractDystonia is an involuntary movement character-ized by sustained， patterned， and repetitive muscle con-tractions of opposing muscles， causing abnormal postures and hyperkinetic jerky movements of affected body parts. This chapter reviews main characteristics of dystonia， classification of dystonias based on spread of symptoms(focal， segmental， hemidystonia， generalized dystonia) and etiology (genetic and acquired dystonias). We discuss main clinical features of the most common types of dystonias， their differential diagnosis， and main therapeutic options， including therapy with botulinum toxins and deep brain stimulation. Additional emphasis is on treatable causes of dystonia， such as levodopa-responsive dystonia and Wilson's disease.

【51】**Keywords Dystonia· Therapy·Botulinum toxin·Deep brain stimulation**

【52】Dystonia is defined as involuntary， sustained， patterned， and repetitive muscle contractions of opposing muscles， resulting in twisting or spasmodic movements， or abnormal postures of the involved body parts.

【107】Primary idiopathic torsion dystonia is an autosomal domi-nant disorder. Although primary idiopathic torsion dystonia may affect various ethnic groups， it is most prevalent in the Ashkenazi Jews， affecting 1 in 6，000 individuals. The mean age at onset is 12.5±8.2 years. The onset， however， is rare after the age of 29. In primary idiopathic torsion dystonia， the DYTI gene mutation on chromosome 9q has been known. The penetrance rate is around 30-40 %， and the only abnor-mality is a deletion of one of a pair of GAG triplets in the ATP-binding protein， torsin A.

【108】The symptoms of primaryidiopathic torsion dystonia begin in a leg or arm and spread to the larynx or neck. When primary idiopathic torsion dystonia starts in a leg， it may progress to generalized dystonia in majority of cases. However， when it starts in an arm， it may progress to general-ized dystonia in about half of the cases. With leg involvement， action dystonia results in an abnormal twisting of the leg when the patient walks forward， even though running， walk-ing backward， or dancing may still be normal. Patients may find it difficult to place the heel on the ground， due to the affected distal muscles. As primary idiopathic torsion dysto-nia progresses， the movements may appear when the leg is at rest； the foot is usually plantar flexed and turned inwards.

【109】With arm involvement， primary idiopathic torsion dystonia can interfere with writing and other activities. With progres-sion， the dystonia may be present even when the arm is at rest， and the dystonia may spread to the other arm or occa-sionally to the neighboring body parts.

【111】With time the primary idiopathic torsion dystonia may spread to other parts of the body， proceeding from focal to segmental to generalized dystonia. The trunk may develop abnormal posture， with speech problems and facial grimac-ing， albeit infrequently. Although muscle power and tone may be normal， the involuntary movements interfere with daily activities. The rate of progression of dystonia is variable and may be most severe within the first 5-10 years. Spasms may cause a marked distortion of the body.

【112】_2.3.2 Primary Idiopathic Dystonia (DYT-6)_

【113】This is the second most common form of dystonia， caused by mutations in the THAPl gene on chromosome 8p. It can cause generalized， segmental， and focal dystonia. It was first reported in families with the onset in the second decade and the onset of dystonia in the extremities， similar to DYT-1. However，subsequent genetic analysis identified patients with craniocervical onset， including isolated focal dystonia，laryn-geal dystonia， or blepharospasm； their age of onset varied from the second to sixth decades.

【114】2.3.3 Dopa-Responsive Dystonia

【115】Around 10 % of patients with childhood-onset dystonia may have dopa-responsive dystonia or Segawa disease. Dopa-responsive dystonia may manifest between ages 6 and 16， although symptoms may occur at any age. Dopa-responsive dystonia affects girls four times more than boys and is not known to have a higher occurrence in any specific ethnic groups. Dopa-responsive dystonia is different from other child-hood dystonias due to the presence of cogwheel rigidity， brady-kinesia， impaired postural reflexes， and hyperreflexia， mainly in the legs. Patients have diurnal fluctuations with improvement of symptoms after sleep and deterioration as the day goes on.

Distinguishing dopa-responsive dystonia from primary idiopathic torsion dystonia is important due to its good|删除0换行|response to levodopa. Patients respond to low doses of levodopa. In childhood it may resemble cerebral palsy， and with onset in adults， it resembles parkinsonism. The main causes of dopa-responsive dystonia are various mutations of the gene for GTP cyclohydrolase I (GCHI)，located at chro-mosome 14q22.1， and genetic label dopa-responsive dysto-nia is DYT5. This trait is transmitted in anaautosomal dominant fashion. There is no loss of neurons within the substantia nigra pars compacta， but the cells may be imma-ture with little neuromelanin. There is significant reduction of dopamine in the striatum in dopa-responsive dystonia； hence， it is a neurochemical rather than a neurodegenera-tive disease.

【117】Atypical cases of dopa-responsive dystonia may be inher-ited in an autosomal recessive pattern with mutations in the gene for tyrosine hydroxylase， and the dystonia-parkinsonism starts in infancy or early childhood in these cases.

【118】The differential diagnosis of dopa-responsive dystonia includes juvenile parkinsonism. Fluorodopa positron emis-sion tomography is normal dopa-responsive dystonia，whereas in juvenile parkinsonism，reduction of fluorodopa uptake in the striatum may be seen. The starting dose of levodopa/car-bidopa for dopa-responsive dystonia is 12.5/50 mg two or three times a day. 【16】#### Introduction

【17】Myotonia is a clinical phenomenon and the cardinal feature of myotonic muscle disorders. It is the sustained involuntary contraction of a group of skeletal muscle fibers following voluntary muscle contraction (action or grip myotonia) or mechanical stimulation (percussion myotonia). The impaired relaxation of muscle from myotonia can lead to symptoms of stiffness, tightness, cramping, or pain. Clinical myotonia is the cumulative result of electrical hyperexcitability of individual muscle fiber membranes. Neurophysiologic myotonia is captured on needle electromyography (EMG) as repetitive spontaneous muscle fiber discharges with a characteristic waxing and waning frequency and amplitude .

【18】通用删除16(英):<u>Figure 47.1 Myotonic discharge showing variation in amplitude and frequency. Myotonic discharges are spontaneous discharges of single muscle fibers with either a positive wave or brief spike morphology, wax and wane in frequency (20--150 Hz) and amplitude (10 μv to 1 mv), and produce a characteristic dive-bomber sound.</u>

【19】Myotonia can occur in any skeletal muscle. It most commonly affects the distal hand muscles, but can also involve the eyelids, tongue, and legs. Patients often complain of symptoms immediately after initiating muscle activity. They may describe the inability to release their grip after handshake or tight grip, trouble opening their eyelids after a period of rest, and difficulty climbing stairs after sitting. While myotonia is often a presenting, non-disabling symptom, the related cramping and stiffness are major complaints throughout the course of the disease. On physical examination, action myotonia can be elicited by isotonic muscle contraction. The patient is asked to tightly grip and release the examiner's fingers. The myotonia is evident through the delayed and slow release of grip. Percussion myotonia is a prolonged muscle contraction after mechanical tap of the muscle with a reflex hammer. Percussion of the thenar eminence results in prolonged abduction of the thumb, and percussion of the forearm extensor mass while the wrist is hanging down results in prolonged extension of the wrist/fingers. Striking the tongue may elicit contraction in the form of the napkin ring sign. The “warm-up phenomenon,” where myotonia improves with exercise or repeated efforts, can be demonstrated in involved muscles.

【20】The myotonic muscle diseases are divided into dystrophic and non-dystrophic disorders  and can be distinguished by their clinical features , aided by the patterns of compound muscle action potential abnormality on the short and long exercise tests. Serum creatine kinase (CK) is usually normal or slightly elevated in these disorders. The non-dystrophic myotonias are a genetically heterogeneous group of muscle channelopathies involving the chloride (myotonia congenita) or sodium (paramyotonia congenita, hyperkalemic periodic paralysis, K \+ \-aggravated myotonias) channels. The dystrophic myotonias, myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) and type 2 (DM2), are expanded repeat disorders caused by an RNA-mediated disease mechanism with myotonia, progressive muscle atrophy, and multi-system involvement. Electrical myotonia, usually without clinical myotonia, can be seen in myotoxicity (statins, colchicine), other myopathies (acid maltase deficiency, polymyositis), or even associated with severe denervation. A number of conditions will need to be considered in the differential diagnosis of true myotonia by virtue of their association with muscle stiffness, cramping, or delayed relaxation. These include myophosphorylase deficiency (McArdle's disease; glycogenosis type V), hypothyroid myopathy (Hoffman's disease), sarcoplasmic reticulum-Ca 2+ ATPase deficiency (Brody's disease), acquired neuromyotonia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, tetanus, stiff person syndrome, and dysferlinopathies. These will be distinguished by their associated clinical and electrophysiologic features , and the absence of myotonia on needle EMG despite the presence of delayed muscle relaxation (pseudomyotonia) in some of these disorders.

【25】#### Dystrophic myotonias

【26】DM1 and DM2 are autosomal dominantly inherited expanded repeat disorders with myotonia, multi-organ involvement, and progressive muscle atrophy and weakness. DM1 is the most common myotonic disorder in adults, and is caused by expansion of the CTG repeats within the 3′ untranslated region in the DMPK gene on chromosome 9, which leads to nuclear retention of mutant RNA and subsequent RNA toxicity. In successive generations the phenomenon of genetic anticipation is often observed and is associated with instability of the repeat sequence. DM1 is a multi-system disorder that affects skeletal and smooth muscle as well as the eye, heart, endocrine, and central nervous systems. Myotonia, muscle stiffness, and muscle cramping are cardinal features. Muscle weakness and atrophy progress in a distal to proximal pattern. Respiratory muscle involvement, abnormal sleep architecture, hypercapnia, sleep apnea, and respiratory failure are late features. Cardiac conduction defects are common and contribute to patient mortality and risk for sudden death. Iridescent posterior subcapsular cataracts are often seen on slit lamp examination. Central nervous system involvement is frequent and manifests as concrete thinking, depression, low IQ, and apathy. Congenital myotonic dystrophy (CMD) affects infants born to mothers with DM1. Clinically they suffer from severe systemic involvement including hypotonia, mental retardation, cardiomyopathy, and respiratory insufficiency. The characteristic clinical myotonia is absent in infants, but may appear later on in childhood.

【39】Therapeutic interventions in the dystrophic myotonias are currently targeted towards symptom management. However, many advances have been made in understanding the complex pathophysiology of DM1 and will hopefully lead to novel therapeutic options for the dystrophic myotonias.

【40】#### Non-dystrophic myotonias

【41】The non-dystrophic myotonias (myotonia congenita, paramyotonia congenita, hyperkalemic periodic paralysis, K \+ \-aggravated myotonias), are pure skeletal muscle diseases, and do not involve the heart, brain, eye, or other organs. Muscle atrophy and weakness are not prominent features of these diseases. The major clinical complaints are muscle stiffness as a consequence of the myotonia, as well as pain and fatigue. The non-dystrophic myotonias are clinically distinguished by the presence or absence of periodic paralysis and other clinical features .

【42】Myotonia congenita is the most common inherited muscle channelopathy and is caused by mutations in the skeletal muscle chloride channel gene ( CLCN1 ) on chromosome 7q. It can be inherited in either an AD (Thomsen's disease) or AR (Becker's disease) pattern; the recessively inherited disorder tends to be slightly more severe. The chloride channel myotonias are caused by a permanent reduction of the resting chloride conductance of the muscle fiber membranes. Normal chloride conductance is necessary for a fast repolarization of the muscle fiber membranes. When they are disrupted, the muscle fiber membranes stay depolarized causing myotonia, or become hyperdepolarized creating an inexcitable muscle fiber membrane leading to a transient paresis. Myotonia and its related muscle stiffness is the most characteristic clinical feature; it is most pronounced during rapid voluntary movements after a period of rest, and demonstrates the warm-up phenomenon. Severe cases may develop muscle hypertrophy. Patients with recessive myotonia congenita typically experience a transient weakness on initiating an action, which is only rarely seen in dominant myotonia congenita.

【43】The sodium channel myotonias (paramyotonia congenita, K \+ \-aggravated myotonia and hyperkalemic periodic paralysis) are allelic, AD disorders caused by point mutations in the skeletal muscle sodium channel gene ( SCN4A ) on chromosome 17q, resulting in a long-lasting depolarization of the muscle fiber membrane. The depolarization can initiate successive action potentials, leading to myotonia. Paramyotonia congenita is characterized by episodic muscle cramping and weakness, which are precipitated by cold and exercise. Facial, tongue, and hand muscles are most affected, and eyelid myotonia is almost always present. Paradoxical myotonia is a frequent feature of paramyotonia congenita, wherein myotonia worsens with continued exercise (opposite of the warm-up phenomenon). Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis may be accompanied by myotonia in some cases, although episodic paralysis is usually the dominant feature. The attacks of paresis are frequent, brief, and often precipitated by rest after exercise, stress, and ingestion of certain foods. In K \+ \-aggravated myotonia patients have myotonia that is exacerbated by potassium ingestion, without any sensitivity to cold. There is no associated weakness or attacks of paresis, and most notably patients respond to acetazolamide or mexilitine.

【44】Many patients with non-dystrophic myotonic muscle disease who experience mild myotonia can manage their disease without medication. Severe, functionally limiting myotonia may require symptomatic treatment, usually with antiarrhythmics (mexilitene), antiepileptics (phenytoin; carbamazepine), or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.

【45】#### Case vignette

【46】A 41-year-old Lieutenant who was recently called back to active duty presented with progressive difficulty manipulating his gun. Over the past few months it had become increasingly difficult to release his clenched fingers from the trigger after firing. Since the age of 25 he has had mild difficulties manipulating fine objects, and hand stiffness. He had no weakness in his arms or legs, and no abnormal sensations of numbness and tingling. He stumbles frequently, but there have been no falls. He has a history of diabetes. His mother died due to sudden death at the age of 50. His 15-year-old son has difficulty texting for prolonged periods of time.

【47】His neurologic examination revealed frontal balding, mild facial weakness, and non-fluctuating ptosis. He had mild weakness and atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of his hands and feet. He was able to toe walk, but was unable to heel walk. Percussion and grip myotonia were elicited on exam. Electromyography revealed myotonic discharges in the abductor pollicis brevis muscle (APB). Genetic analysis revealed an abnormal expansion of CTG repeats in the 19q13.3 DMPK gene, and he was diagnosed with myotonic dystrophy type 1. Further evaluations included a polysomnographic study which revealed the presence of sleep-disordered breathing, an electrocardiogram which revealed bundle branch block, and a slit-lamp examination which revealed posterior subcapsular cataracts.

【48】Ankle--foot orthoses were recommended for assistance with foot weakness. Physical and occupational therapy were recommended for assistance with hand weakness and gait dysfunction. No medications were recommended for his hand stiffness due to the risk of precipitating cardiac conduction defects. He was honorably discharged from duty.

【62】“Nystagmus,” from the Greek meaning “to nod off,” is an involuntary biphasic rhythmic ocular oscillation; while both phases may be slow, at least one phase always is slow. The slow phase is responsible for the initiation and generation of the nystagmus, whereas the fast phase is corrective movements bringing the fovea back on target 通用删除6(英):<u>\[ 1 – 4 \]</u>. Nystagmus interrupts steady fixation and may interfere with vision either by blurring the object of regard, or making the environment appear to oscillate (oscillopsia ), or both.

【63】For clinical purposes, nystagmus is divided broadly into pendular and jerk forms. Either form may be horizontal or, less commonly, vertical. The different waveforms of nystagmus are illustrated in the oculographic diagram . Pendular nystagmus is characterized by a sinusoidal waveform with relatively equal velocities in both directions (A). Jerk nystagmus, named for the direction of the fast phase, is divided into three types on the basis of the slope of the slow phase tracing: constant linear velocity (B), exponentially decreasing velocity (C), and exponentially increasing velocity (D).

【84】Primary non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the testis is a rare dis-ease and accounts for ~9% of testicular tumors (but is the most common malignancy in elderly patients). Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)， the most common type of testicu-lar lymphoma， occurs mostly in patients >60 years old and is clinically characterized by unilateral painless scrotal swelling； high incidence of bilateral involvement (35%)； frequent spread to the skin， central nervous system (CNS)， lung， and Waldeyer’s ring； and aggressive clinical behavior with poor prognosis， especially in patients with advanced disease 通用删除6(英):<u>\[1-10\]</u>. Testis may be rarely involved by mantle cell lymphoma (MCL)， Burkitt lymphoma (BL)， peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL)， not oth-erwise specified， anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL)， and extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma， nasal type (ENKTL).

【99】页码间删除-1:<u>**Differential Diagnosis**</u>

【100】The differential diagnosis of primary testicular DLBCL includes seminoma， chronic orchitis， plasma cell neoplasm， follicular lymphoma (FL； especially grade 3)， extramedul-lary myeloid tumor (EMT； granulocytic sarcoma or mono-blastic sarcoma)， PTCL， ENKTL， blastoid or pleomorphic variantsCofMCL， BL， acutelymphoblastic leukemia(B-ALL or T-ALL)， and secondary testicular involvement by systemic lymphomas. Seminoma shows nests of tumor cells with fibrous septa and admixture of mostly small lymphocytes. Tumor cells are positive for placental alka-line phosphatase (PLAP) and OCT4， and do not express B-cell markers. Chronic orchitis shows rather pleomorphic inflammatory infiltrate without significant atypia and often with scattered lymphoid follicles. Immunophenotypically， both B and T cells are present. FLs composed of predomi-nantly large- or medium-sized cells (grade 3) may resemble DLBCL，especially with the presence of focal diffuse areas. 【20】Anxiety Disorders

【21】Disorders

【22】Anxiety is a normal human emotion that is often adaptive and is recognized as the anticipation of a prospective threat (that may or may not happen). For example， many ofus may study for an examination because of anxiety about fail-ing (rather than because of a real love of learning). The diagnoses in the “Anxiety Disorders”section of the DSM-5 删除1:<u>(APA， 2013)</u> represent more chronic and ex-treme states of anxiety as well as behaviors developed to forestall anxiety. In any event， the specific diagnoses presented in this section relate to anxiety that is suf-ficiently severe to cause significant clinical distress and/or disruption in psycho-social functioning. Differentiation of anxiety disorders， from one another and other mental disorders (e.g.， depressive disorder with anxious distress) can be accomplished by focusing on “the types of situations that are feared or avoided and the content of the associated thoughts or beliefs”删除2:<u>(APA， 2013， p. 189)</u>. For all the diagnoses mentioned in this chapter supporting criteria require that the anxiety must cause clinically significant distress or impairment， which cannot be the result of either another medical/mental disorder or substance induced.

【23】The first two disorders are more prevalent in children but can occur at any-time in the life cycle. Separation Anxiety Disorder can be diagnosed in adults and children with the only difference being the length of time that the anxiety/fear or avoidance is present with duration criteria being at least one month for children and a minimal of 6 months for adults. The anxiety experienced by the individual is extreme and developmentally inappropriate occurring when separated from home or loved ones/parents/caregivers. For diagnosis， 3 out of8 symptoms (e.g.， excessive distress surrounding separation from home/family) must be present. For example， a child may fear that something “awful” will hap-pen to loved ones if he or she is not present. The child may become so fearful that he or she cannot stay away from home (e.g.， at school or camp) without being extremely upset. Adults experience the same symptoms， but the circumstances may differ. For example， a spouse may worry excessively about their significant other and/or children， to the point that it disrupts their own work life or social relationships. The anxiety associated with being away from home is excessive for the developmental level of the individual. Often， parents misinterpret this disorder as being fear associated with school when， in reality， it is a fear of leaving home or loved ones. Since children with this disorder often come from enmeshed families， it is often difficult for parents to “let go”and allow the child to experience the discomfort necessary in order to overcome this problem. Par-ents may also identify a physiological reason (e.g.， stomachaches) rather than the psychological reason for the problems the child is experiencing 删除1:<u>(APA，2013)</u>.

The other disorder more frequent in childhood (but found in adults as well)， Selective Mutism， is diagnosed when an individual willingly fails to speak in|删除0换行|situations where speech is expected and is not due to lack of language skills. In some children， it appears to be a coping mechanism for dealing with anx-iousness. For diagnosis of this less common disorder， the speech disruption must last at minimum one month (and should not be limited to the first month of school) and must hinder academic or work-related achievement or social/communication skills 删除1:<u>(APA， 2013)</u>.

【25】The next two anxiety disorders are related to better-specified， anticipated fears. Although some clients suffering from these disorders may experience panic attacks ， others may simply feel a height-ened level of anxiety. For example， in Specific Phobias， the client fears some specific object or situation. Consequently， he or she predictably experiences in-creased anxiety or a panic attack whenever exposed to the feared stimuli and coded based on the specific phobic stimuli (e.g.， animal， natural environment). 【33】**Assessment**

【34】When assessing someone whom you suspect may have an anxiety disorder， par-ticular attention will be focused on the person’s fears and worries. Although a thorough history is required to make a diagnosis of a specific anxiety disorder， it may be difficult for clients to present detailed and accurate information. They may deliberately minimize symptoms because of internalized stigma. It may be difficult for them to discern their internal thought processes. They may be embar-rassed by details that， in their minds， are clearly excessive (and perhaps“crazy”).

Because fear and worry are primarily internal processes， consulting collat-eral sources may not be useful， particularly in cases when stigma is high. Clients|删除0换行|may actively hide the details of their anxieties or may minimize the impact of their situation. Significant others may be “fooled" by such strategies or may actively collude in minimization.

【36】It should be noted that， particularly， when panic attacks are involved， col-lateral medical referrals are warranted. Even in situations where the client seems healthy， ruling out serious medical problems is an essential part of the assess-ment process. To aid assessment， both cross-cutting dimensional measures and diagnostic specific severity measures of anxiety have been included in Section III of the DSM-5 删除1:<u>(APA， 2013)</u>. The state anxiety scale is nX intended to measure transitory feelings of nervousness， worry， tension， and/or apprehension. In contrast， the trait anxiety scale reflects individual differences in the characteristic response to stress. The DaT-Scan shows that the putamina (parts of the basal ganglia) did not show an appropriate enhancement of the tracer， which is indicative for any kind of Parkinson’s disease (PD). Moreover the reduced enhancement was bilateral， which does not coincide with idiopathic PD. In idiopathic PD one would expect a unilateral reduction. 【27】**4.3.2Motor impairment and apraxia in corticobasal degeneration or corticobasal syndrome**

【28】**One important neuropsychological difference between PSP and CBD/CBS patients is that the latter may suffer from apraxia. The presence of apraxia is vital because apraxia is not a presenting sign in other neurodegenerative dis-eases. Apraxiaistraditionally subdivided in three subtypes：ideational apraxia， ideomotor apraxia， and limb kinetic apraxia. CBD/CBS apraxia con-cerns the latter two subtypes. Limb kinetic apraxia denotes a disturbance in the melody of movement， mainly of hand movements. This corresponds with dystonia， which is a major motor disorder of CBD/CBS. Ideomotor apraxia refers to a disability to copy a movement or to perform a movement on com-mand without having the related tool available. Ideomotor apraxia can also refer to the inability to show expressive behavior on command. The main symptom of ideomotor apraxia is the parapraxia， which is a distortion of the movement elements. Parapraxia is caused by perseverations or by incorrect imitation based on the direct visual perspective of the hand position and not on the perspective of the person producing the hand position.**

【29】Leiguarda， Lees， Merello， Starkstein， and Marsden (1994) studied the fre-quency of different symptoms in CBD/CBS. Table 4.18 shows that dystonia and apraxia often go hand and hand. Observing dystonia without limb kinetic apraxia is effortless， however， it is hard to differentiate limb kinetic apraxia from dystonia. Cortical sensory loss is another frequent symptom in CBD/CBS. Sensory loss should be tested by asking the patient to close his or her eyes. Then the examiner touches the hands， arms， and legs， with either one or two small sticks and with varying pressure (high vs low)， to see whether the touch can be recognized and distinguished.

【30】**In the same investigation Leiguarda et al. (1994) showed that ideational apraxia was relatively rare in the group of patients. Furthermore most of patients could recognize movements despite being unable to execute verbally instructed movements.**

In partial support of this criticism， over 2，600 children with epilepsy underwent IQ testing at ages 4 and 7as part of the Collaborative Perinatal Project， and early age of onset had little prognostic value with regard to intellectual functioning 删除1:<u>(EHenberg， Hirtz， & Nelson， 1985)</u>. Thus， intelligence did not deteriorate in the|删除0换行|majority of the children with epilepsy in this study. After reviewing the literature to date on mental and psychological deterioration in epilepsy， Lesser， Luders， Wyllie， Dinner， and Morris (1986) concluded that even though epilepsy may have severe social consequences for patients， stud-ies suggest that there is little evidence that it causes cognitive deteriora~tion in most patients. 【13】**Language**

【14】**Although linguistic functions have not been thoroughly scrutinized in epilepsy， a robust finding is that partial complex seizure patients with left temporal lobe foci show mild anomia on visual confrontational naming testss 删除1:<u>删除2:<u>(Hermann & Wyler， 1994； Perrine， Gershengorn， &Brown， 1991)</u></u>. Mayeux， Brandt， Rosen， and Benson (1980) found that left temporal lobe epileptics performed significantly worse on the Boston Naming Test than either right temporal lobe epileptics or pri-mary generalized epileptics， but there were no differences between these groups on the Controlled Word Association Test (F-A-S).Ojemann and Dodrill (1985) reported a significant correlation between the nui-ber of errors on the Reitan-Indiana Aphasia Screening Test from the Halstead-Reitan Battery and the degree of postoperative memory impairment in 13 patients one month after left temporal lobectomy.**

**Herman and Wyler (1988) found no statistically significant differ-ences between patients with left and right temporal lobe epilepsy on any of the seven subtests of the Multilingual Aphasia Examnination 删除1:<u>(MAE； Benton & Hamsher， 1989)</u> either before or after temporal lobectomy. The left temporal lobe epilepsy group did， however， perform in a more impaired fashion on six of seven MAE subtests preoperatively relative to right temporal lobe epileptics. Hermann， Wyler， Steenman， and Richey(1988) reported that the Visual Naming and Controlled Oral Word Association subtests of the MAE were the best overall predictors of ver-bal memory function on the California Verbal Learning Test， and sug-gested that subtle language impairment may be the underlying cause of the verbal learning and memory deficits seen among left temporal lobe epileptics. Using a different sample of temporal lobectomy candidates with intractable partial complex seizures， Hermann， Wyler， and Sornes(1991) replicated their earlier findings of a relative inpairment on all but one of the MAE subtests among left temporal lobe epileptics. Only one preoperative MAE subtest comparison (reading comprehension)|删除0换行|reached statistical significance (dominant teinporal lobe group scoring significantly lower)， but Aural Comprehension and Visual Naming approached statistical significance.**

【16】**Seidenberg and colleagues (1998) exanined the pre-to post-opera-tive changes on MAE Visual Naming and Aural Comprehension and found a significant post-temporal lobectomy effect for Visual Naming only in left temporal epileptics without evidence of mesial temporal lobe sclerosis. The extent of the post-operative verbal memory decline in left temporal lobectomy patients without mesial sclerosis was signifi-cantly greater than the decline in either visual naming or the verbal-conceptual factor of the WAIS-R. This suggests that although mild language deficits may contribute to the verbal memory deficits seen in left temporal epileptics， it cannot be the only cause. That is， there is probably dysfunction in mnemonic neural circuitry that is independent of disruption of the language areas of the brain.**

【17】**Loring， Meador， and Lee (1994) examined the early (days) and late(1-year) effects of left and right temporal lobectomy on the MCG Aphasia Screening Test， a bedside examination of language including visual confrontational naming， descriptive or responsive naming， aural comprehension， letter and animal fluency， sentence repetition， read-ing， and writing to dictation. Acutely， the left temporal lobe group displayed deficits on visual naming， descriptive naming， reading， and writing while letter and animal fluency declined in both groups. One year after temporal lobectomy there were no pre-to post-operative changes on any of the language subtests of the MCG Aphasia Screening Test， and letter fluency performance was significantly higher than at the preoperative or acute assessments reflecting the beneficial effects of seizure control on this task. Saykin and colleagues (1995) reported that there was no significant post-operative decline in language functions among left temporal lobectomy patients with early onset of seizures or early risk factors for development of seizures. The authors speculated that early brain insult or dysfunction may result in the intracerebral reorganization of language functions which， in turn， may have a protec-tive effect against the development of post-lobectomy anomia.**

**These results indicate that there is often some form of subtle lan-guage deficit in patients with left temporal lobe epilepsy even though there is usually no evidence of interictal aphasia. Although subtle， mild language impairments observed among left temporal lobe epileptics may contribute to verbal learning and memory problems， linguistic deficits are not the sole cause of poor memory. Finally， it appears that|删除0换行|the left temporal lobectomy patients most at risk for post-operative language problems (notably mild naming deticits) are those without mesial temporal lobe sclerosis.**

【19】**Visual-Perceptual and Spatial Functions**

【20】**Few research studies have specifically addressed visual-perceptual or visual-spatial functions in epilepsy. Milner (1954) reported that right temporal lobe epileptics performed significantly worse than left tenipo-ral lobe epileptics on the McGill Picture Anomalies Test (which required the patient to pick out an incongruous object from a meaning ful scene) both before and after temporal lobectomy. This selective deficit was interpreted as being due to deficient visual-perceptual analy-sis. Kimura (1963) presented overlapping familiar and unfamiliar fig-ures tachistoscopically to patients with left and right temporal lobe seizure onset，both before and after temporal lobectomy， and found the right temporal lobe group was impaired on the perception of the unfa-miliar， but not the familiar， stimuli. This visual-perceptual impairment of right temporal lobe epileptics relative to left temporal lobe epileptics reached statistical significance both pre-and post-operatively. It was sug gested that disruption of right temporal lobe pathways， by either repeat-ed seizures or lobectomy produced difficulties in visually analyzing unfamiliar or difficult to verbalize stimuli. Kimura also found that right temporal lobectomy patients displayed visual-perceptive deficits on Mooney Closure Faces. Contrary to these results， Milner (1968) did not find any differences between left and right temporal lobectomy patients in recognizing unfamiliar faces with no delay interval between stimulus presentation and recognition.**

**Neither left nor right temporal lobe epileptics were impaired in their ability to copy the Taylor Complex Figure， and both groups obtained similar scores 删除1:<u>(Taylor，1969)</u>. Although Loring， Lee， and Meador (1988) also obtained equivalent scores in left and right temporal lobe epilep. tics on the Rey Complex Figure using the scoring criteria outlined in Lezak (1995)， right patients had significantly more qualitative errors， such as distortion or misplacement. Chelune， Naugle， Luders， and Awad (1991) found no significant preoperative differences between left and right temporal lobe epileptics on a variety of nonverbal tasks including WAIS-R PIQ Visual Organization Test， Seashore Rhythm Test， and the Spatial Relations score from the Reitan-Indiana Aphasia Screening Test. Seidenberg and colleagues (1998) reported no pre-to|删除0换行|post-operative impairments on the Facial Recognition Test or Judgment of Line Orientation in epilepsy patients who underwent temporal lobeciomy.**

【22】**Patients with epilepsy may have mild deficits on some visual-percep tive and visual-spatial tasks. As with all other cognitive domains， these impairments depend upon the severity of epilepsy and the location and type of neuropathological process. The more recent and methodologi-cally well controlled studies have generally not found significant percep-tual or spatial deficits among patients with right temporal lobe epilepsy. If such deficits are obtained in idiopathic temporal lobe epilepsy， they most likely reflect poor seizure control or adverse medication effects.**

【23】**Executive or Frontal Lobe Functions**

【24】**Mental functions that have been associated with the frontal lobes include complex problem solving， abstraction， planning， flexibility and the capacity to shift mental set， inhibition and other aspects of self-regu-lation and motivation. Epileptic patients with identified etiologies may show the expected symptoms depending upon whether their lesion is located in the dorsolateral frontal lobe， orbital-frontal region， or in the mesial aspect of the frontal lobe. Idiopathic epileptic patients tend to have less virulent and more subtle etiologies such that many partial complex epilepsy patients with focal frontal lobe seizure onset will not show any frontal lobe mental symptoms.**

【9】Emergency Considerations Isolation， stigma， and functional impairment are all too common in individuals suffering from the mental disorders contained in this chapter. When treating individuals with an obsessive-compulsive re-lated disorder (OCRD)， which often overlap with other diagnoses， it is im-portant to address suicide risk. Although the research on OCD and suicide is limited and at times contradictory， assessment of the suicide ideation and intent may be warranted. One study of suicide and OCD by Kamath， Reddy， and Kandavel (2007) reported a 10-27% lifetime suicide attempt rate as well as high rates of suicidal ideation. Similarly， Fawzy and Hashim (2011) concluded that suicidal ideation in OCD is more prevalent than was earlier believed， and it is strongly interrelated with sociodemographic factors. Yet another study found that although suicide behavior in OCD is not highly common， it poses a greater risk in individuals who were diagnosed with OCD， unmarried， with comorbid depression and symmetry/ordering obsessions and compulsions 删除1:<u>(Alonso et al.，2010)</u>. These results are consistent with the findings on other OCRDs. Studies on BDD show it is often associated with high rates of suicidalideation， attempts， and completion at 45 times the rate of the general population 删除1:<u>(Phillips， 2007)</u>.

【10】In the National Guidelines Clearinghouse’s “Practice guideline for the treat-ment of patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder” published by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality， enhancing the safety of the patient with OCD is paramount to practice as these individuals have a higher suicide attempt rate than the general population. They also point out that individuals with OCD rarely perpetrate violent behavior. Assessing the risk of self-harm and suicide from intrusive thoughts and compulsions (i.e.， Do they have an active plan and intent?) can be challenging particularly if accompanied by co-occurring disorders and poor insight. Care must be taken when evaluating individuals for suicide risk as aggressive/sexual themes can often be misinterpreted as indicating risk.

【11】Cultural Considerations

【12】Although the prevalence and clinical features of OCD is relatively equal world-wide 删除1:<u>(Staley & Ward， 1995)</u> research shows that ethnic minorities (African Americans， Asians， and Hispanic/Latinos) in the United States are less likely to re-ceive treatment for OCD and are underrepresented in OCD clinical trials 删除1:<u>删除2:<u>(Chow， Jaffee， & Snowden， 2003； Himle et al.， 2008； Williams， Powers， Yun， & Foa，2010； Williams， Turkheimer， Schmidt，& Oltmanns， 2005)</u></u>. The same was found for ethnic minority children. Without treatment， ethnic minorities are more likely to suffer lifelong disability and impairment despite effective treatments.

An explanation for this access to treatment disparity between the majority and minority populations may be a function of cultural， racial， and ethnic dif-ferences. Cultural factors can influence the mental health of racial/ethnic minori-ties， especially in terms of help-seeking behaviors. Williams，Domanico，Marques， Leblanc， and Turkheimer (2012) found that major treatment barriers for African Americans included fear and distrust about the therapist and therapeutic process as well as the stigma and judgment associated with a diagnosis of a mental dis-order. For many Asian and Hispanic Americans， cultural barriers include stigma and shame as well as language and acculturation barriers and traditional family structure that relies on the family to handle problems without outside assis-tance 删除1:<u>(APA， 2007a， b； Kramer， Kwong， Lee， & Chung， 2002)</u>. Also， considering|删除0换行|the vast cultural heterogeneity of African/Black， Hispanic/Latino， and Asian pop-ulations the lack of culturally appropriate services may also be a deterrent.

【14】Another possibility for this disparity may be measurement bias and the possibility that differences in responses to questions about mental health are a function of cultural/racial/ethnic differences. Research suggests that current self-report instruments for OCD may be inadequate for assessing diverse racial/ethnic groups. Replicating earlier studies， it was demonstrated that African Americans score significantly higher on levels of cleaning symptoms using contamination scales of OCD than European Americans (even higher than those reporting a diagnosis of OCD). Often， this symptom expression did not meet the diagnostic criteria for OCD， as it did not always result in reports of anxiety or distress删除1:<u>(Williams et al.， 2005)</u>. Research on this self-reporting difference suggests that it should not be attributed to greater psychopathology in African Americans and may be the result of correlations with nonpathological attitudes. In effect， a greater concern with cleanliness may be a cultural norm for African Americans删除1:<u>(Williams & Turkheimer， 2007)</u>. In general， the most common obsessions are fears of contamination and cleaning/washing compulsions. Implications for prac-tice include a focus on subjective distress and time spent on compulsions rather than specific behaviors 删除1:<u>(Williams， Turkheimer， Magee， & Guterbock， 2008)</u>.

【15】Although the core clinical features of OCRDs appear independent of cultural variations， cultural differences can be found in the presentation and expression of illness symptoms/behaviors. However， information is limited on how cul-ture， race， and ethnicity can impact symptom expression in these disorders. For example， studies of highly religious cultures (Christian， Jewish， Muslim) from around the world (Middle East， Asia， and the United States) have demonstrated that religion and culture can affect OCD symptom expression manifesting in religious obsessions and compulsions including cleaning rituals and compulsive praying. In religious cultures， religion can provide an excellent method of con-cealment for ritualizing. However， it is important to note that religion does not increase the prevalence of OCD in the very religious； rather it is often the outlet of choice for symptom expression.

【16】Although the prevalence of BDD and clinical features appears to be similar in many different cultures around the world (approximately 1-2%) and has been documented for over a century， research on cultural， racial， and ethnic differences is very limited. Some data suggest that cultural factors (i.e.，appear-ance preferences) may influence symptom presentation in BDD. For instance， Phillips (2004) found eyelid concerns and the fear of displeasing others by being unattractive a common symptom in Japan but rare in Western countries. As with all disorders， clinicians need to be mindful of the possible overlap of symptoms with culture-bound syndromes. For instance， taijin kyofusho and koro， both culture-related syndromes occurring in Japan and southeast Asia have similarities to BDD but differ in duration， fears， and response. As noted in the DSM-5 删除1:<u>(APA， 2013)</u>， a disorder known as shubo-kyofu translated as the phobia of a deformed body， may bear a close resemblance to BDD in terms of symptomatology.

【19】Gender

【20】Gender differences have been reported among the obsessive-compulsive and re-lated disorders. Studies of OCD show that males are more likely to be single， have earlier onset， and a more chronic course with greater impairment. Fur-ther， gender-related social roles may affect the content of obsessions and com-pulsions. Males tend to report more religious/sexual and aggressive symptoms and females more contamination/cleaning symptoms 删除1:<u>(de Mathis et al， 2011)</u>. Research on gender differences in BDD is limited and prevalence ratios by gender vary with data showing more similarities than differences. Males were more likely to be older， single/living alone， have a comorbid substance use disorder with excessive body concerns around thinning hair/balding， genitals， and muscularity. Females tended to have a greater number of body concerns， have comorbid eating disorder with greater distress over excess body hair， and weight/body composition. These concerns carried out in BDD behaviors with males reporting more weight lifting behaviors and women more camouflaging techniques and mirror checking behaviors. Of interest， Phillips， Mena061200rd， andFay (2006) reported inconsistent findings when comparing scores by gender on three BDD severity measures. After controlling for the presence of eating disorders the higher scores found for females on one scale was eliminated. One possible explanation for the higher score by females on some scales may be that the items endorsed were measuring appearance dissatisfaction， which tends to be of greater weight for women than men in our society. In general women tend to endorse more symptoms of BDD than men， and sexual minorities endorsed more symptoms than heterosexuals 删除1:<u>(Boroughs， Krawczyk，& Thompson，2010)</u>. Further， muscle dysmorphia， a variant of BDD is more prevalent in males.

【21】Although hoarding behavior occurs in other psychotic disorders most of the research on this behavior is in relation to OCD (of which it was previously a subtype). These studies find gender differences with males reporting more aggressive， sexual/religious obsessions and with checking compulsions comor-bid with generalized anxiety disorder and tics. Females had more comorbidity including BDD and skin picking 删除1:<u>(Samuels et al.， 2008)</u>. Hair pulling in females was found to have earlier onset， less comorbidity， and more disability than males 删除1:<u>删除2:<u>(Lochner， Seedat， & Stein， 2010)</u></u>. There is very little data available about the gender differences in the remaining disorders.

【11】**Differential Diagnosis：General Princioles**

【12】**The clinical differential diagnosis is always provisional and subject to change as further information from more objective studies such as blood tests and imaging becomes available or as the results of the selected treatments are noted. Spinal conditions that do not have overt neural or dural signs or symptoms are difficult to diagnose except on the provi-sional basis that the selected treatment has its predicted outcome. For example， back pain with somatic pain radiating into the buttock that is not accompanied by neural or dural signs or symptoms could be caused by a number of pathologies. These include a contained disk lesion， a zy-gapophyseal joint dysfunction or inflammation， ligamentous or muscle tearing， injury to the outer anulus fibrosis， compression or other frac-ture， bacterial infection， or neoplasm. Some of these pathologies are much more common than others， and by the law of probabilities alone you would probably be right more often than wrong if you generated two or three diagnoses based on frequency of incidence. Even taking into account the clinical findings， including other aspects of the history and other objective cues， the diagnosis cannot be considered as having100% validity. The best you can do is generate a differential diagnosis in which you have the best confidence. Even imaging studies help only to confirm a clinical diagnosis， given the rate of false positives and neg-atives of MRIs and x-rays.**

【13】**The orthopedic manual therapy examination consists of two parts， a differential diagnostic examination and a biochemical examination. Of the two， the differential diagnostic examination is the more important because it confirms that the patient is appropriate for physical therapy. The biomechanical examination is vital if specific manual therapy or specific exercise is to be administered. For the most part， the differen-tial diagnosis is provisional， depending on further， more objective test-ing or， in retrospect， on the patient recovering with specific treatment. Many therapists look only for red flags on the differential diagnosis ex-amination rather than a specific diagnosis， and although this approach is quite good for precluding inappropriate patients from treatment， it is of little value in the generation of a specific treatment plan，**

【43】**The Subjective Examination**

【44】**The history is perhaps the most important part of the clinical examina-tion of the patient. A careful subjective examination is the tool most likely to uncover red and yellow flags. It will provide the examiner with important information regarding the patient’s problem. Disabilities， symptoms， symptom behavior， irritability， and exacerbating， provoking， and relieving factors can only be ascertained from the subjective exam-ination. A past history of similar symptoms or nonmusculoskeletal con-ditions can be important in arousing the examiner’s suspicions that the patient's problem may not be benign in nature or musculoskeletal in ori-gin. Past treatments and the results of these treatments may indicate the best route to follow for management and what treatments to avoid. The history will afford information regarding the patient’s personality， atti-tude toward his or her problem， and likelihood of compliance with the therapist's instructions regarding exercises， rest， activities， and so forth.**

【45】**The following section of this chapter will look at information gener-ated from the subjective examination of the patient and possible inter-pretations that can be put upon it especially when combined with in-formation garnered from the objective examinations. We will look first at questions that pertain to all regions， spinal and peripheral， and then we will discuss region-specific history taking.**

【155】**Children who are in enough pain to warrant physical therapy should al-ways be viewed with suspicion. For the most part， children recover quickly from minor injuries. They tend not to have the chronic prob-lems that adults suffer from， because they have not yet had the oppor-tunity for cumulative stress or degeneration to take their toll， nor do they normally have the psychological or financial baggage that goes with adults and is capable of complicating an otherwise uncomplicated in-jury， so a child complaining of ongoing pain may have a more severe injury than the trauma would suggest or be suffering from a serious dis-ease. However， now that children are being pushed harder and harder into various forms of competitive sports， we sce more adult types of dysfunction in children than previously. Consequently， a detailed his-tory must be taken not only of the immediate precursor but also of how involved the child is in sports， what if any previous injuries have oc-curred， and how they progressed with treatment.**

【156】**The older patient is， of course， more disposed to degencrative con-ditions， not only of the musculoskeletal system but also of other sys-tems. Cancer and coronary， cerebral， and brainstem infarcts may all be factors in the assessment and treatment of the older patient. The age of the patient will also give an idea of what the range of motion should be when the results of movement tests are considered. The older patient can be expected to be a little stiffer than the younger， because degener-ation increasingly becomes a factor. A young person who is stiff every-where has either very high muscle tone or possibly a systemic joint con-dition. A middle-aged to elderly woman is more likely to have breast cancer than a young one or a man (the median age at diagnosis is 57years and is less than 1 per 100，000 before 25 years of age as compared to 397 per 100，000 at age 80).'**

【157】**Gender**

【158】**This will give some indication as to predisposition. Osteoporosis and gynecologic conditions are either more prevalent in or exclusive to the female； prostatitis， testicular cancer， and so forth are exclusive to the male. Lung cancer is about two and a half times more common among men than among women and has a higher incidence in those with pre-vious pulmonary pathologies such as scleroderma and chronic obstruc-tive pulmonary disease. Breast cancer is about 146 times more com-mon in women than men.**

【159】**A combination of gender and age will often sensitize the therapist more than either alone. A 30-year-old man with low back pain is less likely to have prostate cancer than is a 60-year-old. A middle-aged or elderly female is more likely to have osteoporosis because of the hor-monal deficiencies of menopause.**

【160】**Occupational and Leisure Activities**

【161】**Although the information may give some clues about the underlying cause of the patient's problems， the need to know exactly what the pa-tient does for a living is more important in prognostication and postre-habilitation training. When can the patient go back to work and for how long (full- or part-time)? Will modifications have to be made in the pa-tient’s job description or in the work environment? Will retraining be necessary， and if so when can it begin safely? To answer these ques-tions， in many cases at least， a simple “What do you do for a living?”will not suffice， especially in jobs that are a little more unusual than are those normally encountered by the therapist.**

【162】**Similarly， leisure activities require a detailed description as lo type and intensity. Is this activity likely to have an adverse effect on the pa-tient’s progress， or could it be used as a rehabilitation tool? If the pa-tient insists on continuing with the activity even though the therapist be-lieves it will likely cause problems， then an accommodation must be reached. Delaying the resumption of the activity may help， especially when there is any degree of inflammation present. Reduction in its in-tensity may also be useful. For example， a golfer with thoracic or low back pain can be asked to not drive the ball but to play the shorter shots. This may not be what the patient wants to hear， but it at least allows him or her to pursue the activity even if in a severely modified fashion.**

【68】**Preface**

【69】s the number of volumes of Differential Diag-nosis in Dermatopathology increases， so， too， does the challenge to readers posed by sets of histopathologic simulators. This volume， the fourth in the series， stretches diagnostic acumen further. It is designed for cognoscenti， i.e.， pathologists and dermatologists who have become progressively more confident about resolving problems of differential diagnosis in dermatopa-thology as a consequence ofcompetence derived from mastery of the graded curriculum inherent in Volumes I， II， and III.

【70】Readers can imagine how daunting is the test for us who are commit-ted to raising the bar for differential diagnosis higher and higher. We la-bored long and hard to choose 45 still more valuable sets of diseases that require differentiation from one another in the practice of dermatopathol-ogy. As a histopathologist places a slide on the stage of a microscope，he/she has no notion of whether it will bear another skin tag， molluscum contagi-osum， or seborrheic keratosis， or pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy， interstitial granulomatous dermatitis with arthritis， or syrin-gomatous carcinoma. The last three conditions are among the 90 that form the substance of this work.

Our aim in this volume， as in the preceding three， remains the same， our format is unchanged， and our resolve to share both method and mental-ity is unflagging. 【185】**s recently as the early 1980s， the terms“lamel-lar ichthyosis” and “non-bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma”were considered to be synonymous. Now they are known to represent dis-tinctive diseases clinically， histopathologically， and biochemically. Histo-pathologically， however， the two conditions have several features in com-mon， particularly epidermal hyperplasia with zones of hypergranulosis and orthokeratosis. The major confusion between them does not derive from morphologic similarities， but from the fact that for many years they were thought to be one and the same disease.**

【186】**The key to differentiation of these two diseases turns on the fundamen-tally inflammatory nature of non-bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythro-derma and the non-inflammatory character of lamellar ichthyosis， psoriasi-form changes that are more striking in non-bullous congenital ichthyosis than in lamellar ichthyosis， increased numbers of mitotic figures in the basal layer and slightly above it in the ichthyosiform erythroderma and not in the true ichthyosis， and neutrophils episodically in a parakeratotic corni-fied layer in the erythroderma， but neither neutrophils nor parakeratosis in the ichthyosis.**

【187】**Sections of biopsy specimens of non-bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma taken from children reveal vacuolarization in the cytoplasm in the lower and mid parts of the spinous zone， a less prominent granular zone， and a more marked infiltrate of inflammatory cells than in sections from adults. Because parakeratotic cells are constantly being sloughed from the surface of a lesion of non-bullous congenitalichthyosiform erythro-derma， histopathologic sections may show scant residualparakeratosis.**

【188】**Although both non-bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma and lamellar ichthyosis are inherited in autosomal recessive fashion and both have the Greek root “ichthyos" in their titles， it is now established that they are distinctly different diseases. Lamellar ichthyosis has its onset at birth or in infancy and presents itself with but slight erythema that is most evident in thin zones lodged between plate-like scales. The scales are thick and dark， particularly on the trunk. Severe ectropion is a nearly invariable accompani-ment. Non-bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma， in contrast， generally is marked by prominent erythroderma， but the disease itself is less severe. Accompanying the erythroderma are fine， white scales (except for the legs， where they may be large and plate-like\]， variable alopecia， and slight ectropion. In some women the disease tends to remit at puberty.**

**Any classification of ichthyoses must， perforce， begin with definition of“ichthyosis，" and yet there seems to be little unanimity about such a defini-|删除0换行|tion. That is why one still-accepted classification considers as ichthyoses(1) ichthyoses vulgaris， (2) lamellar ichthyosis (as a synonym for non-bullous ichthyosiform erythroderma)， (3) epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (as _a_ synonym for bbuulllloouuss congenital1ichthyosiform erythroderma)， and(4) psoriatic erythroderma in infants. We define ichthyoses， clinically， as any non-inflammatory disorder in which the scales resemble vaguely those of a fish. For us， therefore， the true ichthyoses are ichthyosis vulgaris， X-linked ichthyosis， lamellar ichthyosis， and acquired ichthyosis. Histopathologically， authentic ichthyoses have as common denominators orthokeratosis and no infiltrate of inflammatory cells. Bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythro-derma is wholly unrelated to non-bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythro-derma. Distinctive keratotic spikes of bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma distinguish it easily clinically from authentic ichthyosis. Bul-lous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma actually is a widespread epi-dermal nevus. The same is true for so-called ichthyosis hystrix， which also is a misnomer. It is not an ichthyosis at all， but a localized expression of bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma， i.e.， an epidermal nevus typified histopathologically by epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. A palmar and plantar keratodermatous analogue of bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma and ichthyosis hystrix is stamped histopathologically by epi-dermolytic hyperkeratosis. Ani oorraall analogue of these three conditionnss is white sponge nevus.

【190】Lamellar ichthyosis fulfills morphologic criteria for true ichthyosis， namely， a non-inflammatory disease accompanied by scales that resemble those of a fish. According to that definition， non-bullous congenital ichthy-osiform erythroderma does not qualify as an authentic ichthyosis because， although it exhibits fish-like scales， it is an inflammatory discase， i.e.， a spongiotic psoriasiform dermatitis. The authentic ichthyoses，i.e.，ichthyosis vulgaris， X-linked ichthyosis， lamellar ichthyosis， and acquired ichthyosis， are not dermatitides. Brocq was correct when he narned the condition“ich-thyosiformn erythroderma”rather than simply ichthyosis.

【191】Many “collodion babies， to wit， newborn infants wrapped in a mem-brane that resembles the skin of a baked apple or a film of collodion， exhibit lamellar ichthyosis once the membrane has been shed. The disorder affect-ing collodion babies does not eventuate in non-bullous congenital ichthyosi-form erythroderma. The skin of collodion babies does not necessarily be-come ichthyotic； it may become perfectly normal.

【192】“Harlequin fetus” is unrelated to either lamellar ichthyosis or non-bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma. It is neither true ichthyosis nor an erythroderma， but a grotesque malformation of the skin in which thick plates give the appearance of armor or the hide of an armadillo. For-merly invariably fatal， some harlequin fetuses have survived as a conse-quence of systemic administration of retinoids.

【1】结尾批量删除-1:<u>**Since many CFS symptoms overlap with depression， differential diagnosis is often a complex process. However， there are soine key fea-tures of each illness to keep in mind when completing a diagnostic evaluation. First， infectious symptoms and a sudden ilness onsei are more characteristics of CFS than of depression. Moreover， although sleep disturbance is common in both disorders， the sleep disorder asso-ciated with depression is carly morning awakening that is often not seen in CFS. Psychological presentation can be a key feature differenti-ating the disorders. Specifically， low mood， feelings of guilt， self-reproach， and an internal illness attribution suggest that a depressive disorder is present. The neuropsychological characteristics of the two disorders are highly similar， with deficits primarily in attention/con-centration and information processing efficiency. Thus， the neuropsy chological evaluation alone may not yield sufficient information for differential diagnosis，**</u>

【2】结尾批量删除-1:<u>**Fatigue can be viewed as either a symptom of an illness (e.g.， depression) or as an illness itself (i.e.， CFS). This multidimensional view of fatigue as both a syiptom and an illness often complicates differential diagnosis. As such， a differential diagnostic determina tion based on the symptom of fatigue alone is inappropriate. Fatigue as an illness is a concept that is still evolving and remains， as yet， poor-ly understood.**</u>

【1】**Because the treatment methods of these conditions are so different， i.e.， systemic antibiotics administered for toxic shock syndrome and systemic corticosteroids given for severe erythema multiforme， accurate diagnosis of histologic sections is imperative if proper therapeutic measures are to be instituted. Accuracy in diagnosis can be accomplished by paying heed to the contrasting features listed in the columns on the first page of this chap-ter.**

【2】**Toxic shock syndrome is differentiated histologically from erythema multiforme principally by the presence of a mixed-cell infiltrate， within which there are neutrophils in the dermis and in the epidermis， particularly in foci of spongiosis and ballooning. In contrast， lymphocytes are present in the dermis and epidermis of erytherna multiforme. Only if there are broad zones of necrosis in the epidermis of erythema multiforme are neutrophils altracted chemotactically to it. Eosinophils may be present in toxic shock syndrome， but not as a rule in erythema multiforme.**

【3】**The toxic shock syndrome is characterized clinically by broad， flat patches of redness that may be widespread and that in time become scaly and crusted. Conjunctivitis and glossitis are common adjuncts， but they do not occur in the absence of cutaneous lesions. In contrast， erythema multi-forme may vary from involvement solely of mucous membranes to wholly of the skin. The skin lesions themselves may be few and confined to the palms and soles or they may be so widespread that erythroderma results. Blisters tend to form atop zones of redness and may be tense vesicles or flaccid bullae. The classic concentric rings oferythema multiforme have been com-pared to an iris， marksman's target， or bull’s cye， but these characteristic lesions are not invariable.**

**The toxic shock syndrome is caused by an exotoxin produced by certain|删除0换行|strains of Staphplococcus aureus， namely， Phage Group I. These organisms may proliferate in many parts of the body， but the most common site has been the vagina of women who use particular types of tampons to absorb products of menstruation. In contrast， severe erythema multiforme is usu-ally caused by a drug taken systemically， but in many instances there is no proven cause，**

【5】**Both the toxic shock syndrome and erythema multiforme may be so severe that the skin of afflicted patients may look as if they had been scalded. The differential diagnosis of the appearance of scalded skin also includes pemphigus vulgaris， a suprabasal blistering disease associated with acantholytic cells， and the staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome， a subcor-neal blistering disease in which there also are acantholytic cells. The cause of pemphigus vulgaris is not known， but circulating antibodies in serum directed against intercellular substance seem to be responsible for the ap-pearance of blisters. The staphylococci responsible for the sealded skin syn-drome differ from those that cause the toxic shock syndrome， belonging to Phage Group II， type F.**

【46】ICHEN planus and lichenoid discoid lupus ery-thematosus have many histologic features in common， among them hyper- _\_11\_.1_ keratosis and plugging of follicles by cornified cells， hypergranulosis， at leastfocal irregular epidermal hyperplasia， necrotic keratinocytes， vacuolar alter-ation along the dermo-epidermal junction， a lichenoid infiltrate of lympho-cytes in the papillary epidermis that obscures the dermo-epidermal junc-tion， a perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate， and melanophages in the papillary dermis.

【47】The feature that is most important in differentiating these two condi-tions is a thickened basement membrane at the junction of the epidermis and dermis (and sometimes at the junction of follicular infundibula and the dermis) in discoid lupus erythematosus. A thickened basement membrane is found in but two conditions in the skin， namely， discoid lupus erythe-matosis and dermatomyositis. Although there are many conditions with lichenoid infiltrates of lymphocytes besides lichen planus and discoid lupus erythematosus (for example， lichen planus-like keratoses， lichenoid photo-dermatitis， lichenoid drug eruptions， and the lichenoid purpura of Gougerot and Blum)， only lichenoid discoid lupus erythematosus is associated with a thickened basement membrane. That membrane is usually seen readily in sections stained by hematoxylin and eosin， but it is morepronounced in sections stained by PAS. It is also the zone that fluoresces when sections are studied by direct immunofluorescence. When studied by electron micros-copy， the thickened basement membrane is found to result from duplication of basal lamina.

【48】Although the lymphocytic infiltrate in lichen planus is usually around the blood vessels of the superficial plexus and that of discoid lupus erythern-atosus is around those of both the superficial and the deep plexuses， these findings are variable. Occasionally， lesions of lichen planus may show in-volvernent of both plexuses， and evolving lesioris of discoid lupus erythema-tosus may be confined to the superficial plexus，

【49】The crucial features that differentiate lichen planus from all other li-chenoid dermatitides are the compact orthokeratosis that is virtually devoid of parakeratosis and the wedge-shaped zones of hypergranulosis that form around epithelial structures of adnexa within the epidermis， that is， hair follicles (acrotrichia) and eccrine ducts (acrosyringia).

Clinically， lichen planus is characterized by flat-topped， polygional pur-plish papules that are notoriously pruritic. Persistent rubbing of the lesions of lichen planus， especially those on the lower extremities， induces the changes of hypertrophic lichen planus， i.e.， lichen simplex chronicus super-|删除0换行|imposed upon lichen planus. When lesions of lichen planus have largely resolved in time， the condition is termed atrophic lichen planus. When the pathologic process is accelerated， there may be vesicles of “bullous"lichen planus. Lesions of lichen planus may affect mucous membranes， hair folli-cles (lichen planopilaris)， and nails； in these sites， the lesions usually have characteristic distinguishing signs.

【51】Discoid lupus erythematosus， like lichen planus， has many different aspects. Early lesions are reddish macules that become papules and then plaques. As the process evolves， follicles become plugged by cornified cells and the lesions themselves become hyperkeratotic and hyperpigmented. In time， there is atrophy accompanied by telangiectases. Lesions that are rubbed persistently may be hyperkeratotic andresolved lesions may be atrophic. Mucous membranes may be affected， hair follicles may be in-volved with resultant permanent alopecia， and the nail units， especially the posterior nail fold， may also show signs of the discase in the form of hypo-pigmentation， telangiectasis， and atrophy.

【52】The sites of predilection for discoid lupus erythemnatosus are quite dif-ferent from those of lichen planus. Lesions of discoid lupus erythematosus often occur on sun-exposed sites， whereas lesions of lichen planus do not. It may be that the “butterfly blush，"i.e.， the patches of erythema on malar cminences of patients with.systemic lupus erythematosus， is actually an evanescent stage of discoid lupus erythematosus. Although the lesions of the latter condition often resolve with scarring， they do not invariably proceed to atrophy and may heal with no residual changes.

【53】Lastly， it must be emphasized that discoid lupus erythematosus， like lichen planus， is a skin disease. Systemic lupus erythematosus， unlike lichen planus， is a disease that affects internal organs. Discoid lupus erythema-tosus can be but one of many cutaneous manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus， but most patients who have discoid lupus erythematosus never develop systemic lupus erythematosus.

LICHEN planus and lichenoid secondary syphilis|删除0换行|have many histologie features in common， including vacuolar alteration at the dermo-epidermal junction， a lichenoid infiltrate composed largely of mononuclear inflammatory cells and admixed sometimes with melano-phages， and a hyperplastic， hyperkeratotic epidermis. Important features that enable differentiation of the two diseases are that in lichen planus rarely is there parakeratosis， the majority of cells in the lichenoid inflamma-lory-cell infiltrate are lymphocytes， and the lesions may show evidence of havingbeen rubbedpersistently， namely， features of lichen simplex chronicus characterized by compact orthokeralosis， hypergranulosis， psori-asiform hyperplasia， and thickening of the papillary dermis by coarse col-lagen bundles in vertical streaks. In lichenoid secondary syphilis， there usu-ally is parakeratosis， the inflammatory-cell infiltrate is predominantly granulomatous (i.e.， histiocytesPpredominate)， there are almost always some plasma cells within the infiltrate， and neutrophils may be present in the epidermis and dermis.

【111】Ordinary lesions of lichen planus have characteristic clinical appear-ances. The flat-toppedpapules often have sharp angles at their peripheries and are violaceous. They may be surmounted by pathognomonic Wickham’s striae， which are whitish， linear streaks that run in different directions on the surface of a single papule. These whitish lines are not usually scaly. There is no consensus about what histopathologic change is responsible for the distinctive clinical finding of Wickham’s striae. We believe that they represent zones of greater orthokeratosis that occur above foci of wedge-shaped hypergranulosis.

Certain anatomic sites are predilective for lichen planus. Flexures ofthe wrists， the glans penis， and buccal mucosa are classic sites of involvement， although any site of skin or mucous membrane may be affected. The thin， lacy， white patches on the buccal mucosa and white plaques on the tongue are identifiable histologically as lichen planus because they have the same characteristic features as does lichen planus in the skin. The disease is gen-erally self-limited， whether on skin or mucous membranes， usually remit-ting within 18 months， but occasionally lasting for years. Exceptions are the prolonged destructive lichen planus of the nails， the scarring alopecia of lichen planus on the scalp， and the erosive， scarring form of the disease that tends to involve palms and soles. A deep hyperpigmentation may be present for months or years after resolution of the papules of lichen planus， but eventually， normal coloration returns， generally without scarring. When slight scarring does occur in the papillary dermis of resolving lesions， the|删除0换行|clinical condition is termed atrophic lichen planus. When there is lichen simplex chronicus superimposed on a lesion of lichen planus， the condition is referred to as hypertrophic lichen planus.

【113】In lichenoid secondary syphilis， the cruption consists of oval， usually scaly， slightly reddish lesions， the color of which depends in large part on the background color of the normal skin. What appears "ham-colored”on a white background may be violaceous on a brown background. At times， smaller papular lesions of secondary syphilis may be nearly indistinguish-able from those of lichen planus. The rather widely accepted adage that lichen planus is pruritic and syphilis is not pruritic is simply not true—the subjective response of itching varies cnormously from patient to patient and exceptions to these rules are common enough to make them useless for differential diagnosis. Histologically， secondary syphilis is usually psoriasi-form and lichenoid. Plasma cells vary in number， but are nearly always present. When they are few， plasma cells are best identified in the deep perivascular infiltrate rather than in the superficial lichenoid zone.

【114】Secondary syphilis is as versatile a mimic histologically as it is clinically. The histologic variations are numerous， including sarcoidal， pseudolympho-matous， spongiform pustular， and follicular forms， to mention but a few. As a rule， spirochetes are found most readily in the epidermis rather than in the dermis， and are demonstrated well with silver stains such as the War-thin-Starry， Levaditi， and Steiner， but immunoperoxidase staining for T. pallidum is most useful. When neutrophils are numerous in the epider-mis， spirochetes will also be numerous. When epithelioid tubercles are pres-ent in the dermis of syphilitic lesions， spirochetes are rarely found. It is important to avoid making an unequivocal diagnosis of secondary syphilis afler analyzing sections stained only by hematoxylin and eosin. Other in-flammatory diseases， especially granulomalous conditions， such as swim-ming pool granuloma， may on occasion be indistinguishable from second-ary syphilis.
